locator: preamble, 'A non-cognitivist, however, may seek to explain how the attitudes or prescriptions expressed in moral claims are justified. (See Hare 1981, Campbell 1985, Gibbard 1990, and Blackburn 1998 for theories of moral justification compatible with non-cognitivism [...].) Indeed, an expressivist may invoke a deflationary conception of truth to support the idea that we can speak of justified moral beliefs that are “true” — without implying that justified moral beliefs accurately represent moral reality.'
interpretation: Read as an option the entry reports for non-cognitivists and expressivists: justified attitudes, called true in the deflationary sense (DEF-TRUTH-MINIMAL), with no claim to represent moral reality. The entry says they 'may' take this line and cites Blackburn 1998 and Gibbard 1990 among theories of justification compatible with non-cognitivism; it does not say that these texts take it, nor that such attitudes are moral knowledge. So it is not recorded as quasi-realism's answer to how we know moral truths: that attribution is open (candidate QUASI-REALISM-MORAL-EPISTEMOLOGY-WITNESS). Attribution reading on a secondary witness: the claim records the option the entry reports, not a thesis of the entry's author. No primary text is pinnable (in copyright, no immutable open text).
